etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English god, from Old English god, originally neuter, then changed to masculine to reflect the change in religion to Christianity, from Proto-West Germanic *god n, from Proto-Germanic *gudą; see there for further origin. Not related to the word good or Persian خدا (xodâ, “god”).

definitions.definition: A deity or supreme being; a supernatural, typically immortal, being with superior powers, to which personhood is attributed.

quote.text: When ancient Greeks had a thought, it occurred to them as a god or goddess giving an order. Apollo was telling them to be brave. Athena was telling them to fall in love.

definitions.definition: A representation of a deity, especially a statue or statuette.
(figurative) Something or someone particularly revered, worshipped, idealized, admired and/or followed.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Philippians 3:19:

definitions.definition: (figurative) A person in a very high position of authority, importance or influence; a powerful ruler or tyrant.

quote.citation: 1959, Percy E. Corbett, Law in Diplomacy, page 105:
quote.text: In 1951 Stalin was a god and the official tone towards the West was one of total antagonism.

definitions.definition: (figurative, informal) A person who is exceptionally skilled in a particular activity.

quote.text: Someone had said he'd look a god in kilts.

definitions.definition: (Internet, roleplaying games) The person who owns and runs a multi-user dungeon.

quote.text: The gods usually have several wizards, or "immortals," to assist them in building the MUD.

quote.citation: 2003, David Lojek, Emote to the Max, page 11:
quote.text: The wizzes are only the junior grade of the MUD illuminati. The people who attain the senior grade of MUD freemasonry by starting their own MUD, with all due hubris, are known as gods.

quote.citation: 1608, William Shakespeare, The Tragedy of Coriolanus, act V, scene III:
quote.text: CORIOLANUS: This last old man, / Whom with a crack'd heart I have sent to Rome, / Loved me above the measure of a father; / Nay, godded me, indeed.

quote.citation: a. 1866, Edward Bulwer Lytton, "Death and Sisyphus".
quote.text: To men the first necessity is gods; / And if the gods were not, / " Man would invent them, tho' they godded stones.

quote.citation: 2001, Conrad C. Fink, Sportswriting: The Lively Game, page 78:
quote.text: "Godded him up" ... It's the fear of discerning journalists: Does coverage of athletic stars, on field and off, approach beatification of the living?

quote.citation: 1595, Edmund Spenser, Colin Clouts Come Home Againe:
quote.text: Then got he bow and shafts of gold and lead, / In which so fell and puissant he grew, / That Jove himselfe his powre began to dread, / And, taking up to heaven, him godded new.

quote.citation: 1951, Eric Voegelin, Dante Germino ed., The New Science of Politics: An Introduction, published 1987, page 125:
quote.text: The superman marks the end of a road on which we find such figures as the "godded man" of English Reformation mystics

quote.citation: 1956, C. S. Lewis, Fritz Eichenberg, Till We Have Faces: A Myth Retold, page 241:
quote.text: "She is so lately godded that she is still a rather poor goddess, Stranger.["]
